query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-temperature sliding (600–800 °C), increasing oxygen availability during post‐deposition annealing promotes the formation of a continuous, load‐bearing oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating that acts as a protective barrier, thereby reducing wear rates and limiting microscopic plastic deformation during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate with minimal oxidation (i.e., processed under low oxygen conditions) resulting in a largely metallic, unoxidized microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a post‐deposition annealing treatment in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (e.g., increased oxygen partial pressure) compared to the baseline inert or low-oxygen treatment.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests conducted at operating temperatures between 600 and 800 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous and adherent oxide layer (likely comprising mixed oxides such as Mn-, Cr-, and Fe-based spinels or corundum phases) that modifies the surface microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature conditions, the enhanced oxygen during annealing facilitates the in-situ formation of a protective oxide film that bears load and acts as a lubricating tribo-layer. This film mitigates plastic deformation at the microscopic scale and helps to reduce adhesive and abrasive wear mechanisms during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, coatings annealed under oxygen-rich conditions will display a lower wear rate (reduced material loss), lower friction coefficients, and less evidence of localized plastic deformation (e.g., reduced delamination and debris accumulation) during sliding tests in the 600–800 °C regime.
generation.baseline: The baseline condition is the coating processed without the enhanced oxygen annealing (i.e., under inert or low-oxygen conditions), which results in a thinner or patchier oxide formation and therefore higher wear rates and more severe microscopic deformation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in the high-temperature regime (600–800 °C) during sliding wear where tribo-oxidation plays a dominant role; its applicability may be limited if the oxide layer becomes overly brittle or if testing conditions (e.g., load, sliding speed) induce different wear mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The exact chemical composition, thickness, and mechanical properties of the oxide phase(s) and how they uniformly influence wear resistance are not fully defined. Additionally, the optimum oxygen partial pressure for beneficial oxide formation versus detrimental oxidation remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings: one set is post-deposition annealed in an oxygen-rich atmosphere and the other in an inert atmosphere (baseline). Subject both sets to high-temperature sliding wear tests at 600–800 °C under identical mechanical loads and sliding speeds while maintaining controlled oxygen partial pressures in the test chamber. Conduct detailed surface and cross-sectional microstructural characterizations (using SEM/TEM, EDS) and nanoindentation tests to assess oxide layer integrity, wear track morphology, and plastic deformation.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., volume loss measured by 3D profiling)
Surface morphology and oxide layer thickness/integrity via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-rich annealed coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in wear rate, a lower friction coefficient, and reduced microscopic plastic deformation (or if they exhibit degraded performance compared to the inert-annealed baseline), then the hypothesis that the enhanced oxide layer governs improved wear resistance and reduced deformation would be falsified.

chosen.technique: high-temperature sliding wear tests paired with electron microscopy and nanoindentation for mapping local deformation
chosen.conditions: tests conducted at 600–800 °C in atmospheres with systematically varied oxygen partial pressures
chosen.why: This move directly tests the hypothesis that in the high-temperature regime the dominant mechanism governing wear resistance and microscopic deformation is the formation of a protective and load-bearing oxide layer. Prior evidence in related high-entropy and multi-principal element alloys suggests that oxidation and its influence on microstructural evolution critically affect wear behavior. By controlling the oxygen partial pressure during thermal processing, the experiment produces a deliberate change relative to a baseline coating condition, thereby allowing prediction of directional changes in wear performance and deformation modes. This approach leverages standard experimental techniques in the field and fills the niche by addressing the mechanistic role of oxide-mediated surface modification.
